title: OOP: Class Methods, Static Methods, Properties

tasks.description: Create a `Person` class with a `@classmethod` called `from_string(cls, s)` that parses 'Alice,30' into a Person. Print the person's name.
tasks.hint:
`@classmethod` receives the CLASS as the first arg (by convention named `cls`).
`def from_string(cls, s): name, age = s.split(','); return cls(name, int(age))`
This is an alternative constructor — very common in Python.
tasks.walkthrough:
`from_string` is called on the class, not an object. It splits the text, converts the age, and calls `cls(...)` to build a Person.
Using `cls` instead of `Person` means subclasses get a working version too.

tasks.description: Add a `@staticmethod` called `is_adult(age)` that returns True if age >= 18. Call it without creating an instance.
tasks.hint:
`@staticmethod` doesn't receive `self` or `cls` — it's just a regular function grouped with the class.
`@staticmethod def is_adult(age): return age >= 18`
Call it directly: `Person.is_adult(20)` — no instance needed.
tasks.walkthrough:
`is_adult` needs neither `self` nor `cls`, only the number passed in.
`@staticmethod` tells Python not to inject anything, so it can be called as `Person.is_adult(20)` with no object.

tasks.description: Use `@property` to create a read-only `full_name` property on a Person class that combines first_name and last_name.
tasks.hint:
`@property` turns a method into an attribute you access without `()` parentheses.
`@property def full_name(self): return f'{self.first_name} {self.last_name}'`
Access: `person.full_name` — not `person.full_name()`
tasks.walkthrough:
`@property` turns the method into a read-only attribute.
`person.full_name` runs the method behind the scenes and gives back the joined name. No brackets needed.

tasks.description: Add a `@property` for `temperature_c` and a setter `@temperature_c.setter` that validates the value is above -273.15.
tasks.hint:
`@property def temperature_c(self): return self._temp`
`@temperature_c.setter def temperature_c(self, value): if value < -273.15: raise ValueError('Below absolute zero!'); self._temp = value`
The `_temp` prefix marks it as private by convention.
tasks.walkthrough:
Reading `t.temperature_c` goes through the getter; assigning to it goes through the setter.
The setter validates and then stores the value in `_temp`. Even the `__init__` assignment goes through the setter, so bad starting values are rejected too.

tasks.description: Add a class variable `count` to track how many instances have been created. Use `__init__` to increment it and a classmethod to retrieve it.
tasks.hint:
`count = 0` at the class level (outside __init__).
In `__init__`: `ClassName.count += 1` (or `type(self).count += 1`).
`@classmethod def get_count(cls): return cls.count` — call as `MyClass.get_count()`
tasks.walkthrough:
`count` is defined on the class, so there's one shared copy.
Each `__init__` bumps `Person.count`, and the classmethod reads it back through `cls`.

lesson.intro:
Three decorators that change what a method inside a class is for. `@classmethod`
works on the class rather than an object. `@staticmethod` is a plain function
that happens to live in the class. `@property` makes a method look like an
attribute. They all show up constantly in real code.

sections.heading: @classmethod: alternative constructors
sections.body:
A classmethod receives the class as its first argument, named `cls` by
convention. The most common use is building an object from a different
kind of input, like a string.

sections.heading: @staticmethod: a function in a class
sections.body:
No `self`, no `cls`. It doesn't use the object or the class; it's just
grouped there because it belongs with them conceptually. Call it on the
class.

sections.heading: @property: computed attributes
sections.body:
A property is read like an attribute, with no brackets, but it runs a method
to produce the value. Useful for values derived from others.

sections.heading: Setters: validating on assignment
sections.body:
Add `@name.setter` to make the property assignable, and put validation
in the setter. The real value is stored under a different name, usually
with a leading underscore.

sections.heading: Class variables: shared by every instance
sections.body:
A variable defined directly in the class body (not in `__init__`) is
shared. Incrementing it in `__init__` counts how many objects have been
made.

watch_out: Calling a property with brackets: `p.full_name()` fails because the result is a string, not a function.
In a setter, storing to `self.temperature_c` instead of `self._temp` calls the setter again forever.
`self.count += 1` on a class variable creates an instance variable instead. Use `Widget.count` or `type(self).count`.
The setter must have the same name as the property.
